column3: Close to the Hebrew.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew says “every man” and shifts from plural “your eyes” to singular “your God” and “your midst.” BSB uses plural “all who.”
Close to the Hebrew.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew separately commands keeping and doing; BSB combines them as “Observe them carefully.” It says “this is your wisdom,” rather than “this will show.”
The Hebrew adjective “near” is plural with “gods”; BSB renders this as singular “a god.” The nation is called “great,” rather than “great enough.”
The Hebrew calls the nation “great,” rather than “great enough.”
The Hebrew addresses one person and says “guard your soul”; BSB uses plural “yourselves.” It explicitly says “sons” and “sons of your sons.”
The Hebrew says “gather the people for Me, and I will make them hear”; BSB renders it as gathering them before Him to hear.
The Hebrew says “to the heart of the heavens” and lists darkness, cloud, and thick darkness; BSB has “to the heavens” and “black clouds.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew calls them “the ten words” and separately states that He wrote them; BSB has “the Ten Commandments” with a relative clause.
The Hebrew says you are crossing over “there”; BSB supplies “the Jordan.”
The Hebrew explicitly says to guard your souls very carefully; BSB condenses this to “be careful.”
The Hebrew distinguishes a carved image, a likeness, and a figure; BSB combines them as an idol of any form or shape.
“Likeness” is repeated twice, and the bird is explicitly “winged”; BSB leaves these details implicit.
The Hebrew repeats “likeness” and explicitly says the waters are “under the earth”; BSB has simply “below.”
The Hebrew says “lift up your eyes” and separately mentions bowing down and serving; BSB condenses the eye image and has “bow down and worship.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew separately negates crossing the Jordan and entering the land; BSB combines them into “cross the Jordan to enter.”
The Hebrew says “this good land”; BSB uses “that good land.”
The Hebrew verb is “commanded,” without an explicit negative; BSB interprets the restriction as “forbidden.” The LORD’s name is repeated in Hebrew, where BSB uses “He.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew begins with a singular person begetting sons and sons of sons, then switches to plural people growing old in the land.
The first prediction of perishing is intensified by repeating its verbal root; BSB expresses it without that emphasis.
The Hebrew says “remain” as a small number of men; BSB uses “survive” with “only.”
The Hebrew says “the work of human hands” and states that they do not see, hear, eat, or smell; BSB condenses the workmanship and uses “cannot.”
The Hebrew begins with plural “you shall seek,” then switches to singular for finding and seeking with the whole heart and soul.
The Hebrew says “at the end of the days”; BSB uses “in later days.”
